source.notes: Folio 5 recto of volume 1 of the illuminated vellum copy in the Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin: the first page of Genesis ('Incipit liber bresith quem nos genesim dicimus. In principio creavit deus celum et terram...'), two columns of 42 lines, with the painted initial I running down the left margin, the running head GENESIS, and the border of flowers, birds and a peacock. 6843 x 9616 px, 30.6 MB, the largest single Gutenberg page on Commons; the uploader describes it as scanned from a facsimile (a printed reproduction of the Berlin leaf), so the colour is that of the facsimile, not a library photograph, and fine detail may show print screen. object.medium: Letterpress printing in Textura type on vellum, with hand-painted initial, border and rubrication
object.description: 'In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth': the opening of Genesis in the first substantial book printed in Europe with movable metal type. Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith's son from Mainz, worked out how to cast thousands of identical letters in a hand mould, how to mix an oil-based ink that would stick to metal, and how to adapt a wine press to print a sheet. Around 1454 and 1455 his workshop printed about 180 copies of the Latin Bible, some on paper and some, like this one, on calfskin, in two volumes of 1,286 pages with two columns of 42 lines each. Only the black text came off the press; the great initial, the border with its birds and peacock, the red headings and the coloured capitals were painted in afterwards by hand, so that no two copies look alike. The whole enterprise was financed by a loan from Johann Fust, who foreclosed before the Bibles were sold. Forty-nine copies survive; this page is from the illuminated vellum copy in Berlin.
facts: Printed in a Textura typeface of some 290 different sorts, including ligatures and abbreviations, to imitate a scribe's hand.
A scribe took about three years to copy a Bible; Gutenberg's press produced the whole edition in about two.
Twenty-one complete copies survive; the Berlin copy is one of about a dozen printed on vellum.
Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini, the future Pope Pius II, saw sheets at Frankfurt in October 1454 and reported that they could be read without spectacles.
